readerTitle: Your booking form loses 92 of every 100 people. Fix it.
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (청소 회사의 가정용 예약 양식과 사무실 청소 견적 양식). 모든 수치는 설명용입니다.
insight: 새는 가입·예약 흐름은 전체를 다시 만들기보다, 사람들이 떠나는 단계를 찾아 그 단계의 마찰, 선택지 수, 기본값을 하나씩 고칠 때 가장 잘 고쳐진다.
misconception: 가입률이 낮으면 디자인을 새로 하거나 할인을 붙이면 된다. 기본값을 회사에 유리하게 설정하면 매출이 늘어난다.

sources.text: 행동경제학과 사용성 분야의 표준 개념 (마찰, 선택 과부하, 기본값 효과)
모든 수치와 회사(Brightway)는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 퍼널 계산: 1,000명 시작 → 900 → 450 → 200 → 80명 예약. 완료율 80 ÷ 1,000 = 8%이므로 100명 중 92명 이탈. 세부 정보 단계에서는 도달한 900명 중 450명(50%)이 떠나므로 카드 제목을 '도달한 사람의 절반'으로 적었습니다.
각 선택지의 결과(이탈 감소, 견적 오류 등)는 실제 측정값이 아니라 설명용 서술입니다. 구체적인 개선 수치를 만들어 넣지 않았습니다.
12개월 계약 자동 체크 선택지는 다크 패턴의 예입니다. 특정 국가의 소비자 보호법 내용은 다루지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Your booking form loses 92 of every 100 people.
body: You run Brightway, a home and office cleaning company. Last month, 1,000 people started the booking form on your website. Only 80 finished.
Your ads are working. Your form is not. For the next few cards, fixing it is your job.

image.label: A leaking funnel with tiny people falling out at each step
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 위에서 작은 사람들이 많이 들어가는 깔때기. 각 마디의 틈으로 사람들이 빠져나가고, 아래로는 몇 명만 나옴. 깔때기 옆에 청소 도구(대걸레, 스프레이). 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where do you start?
body: Your web designer has two free weeks. Your sales lead wants a discount banner. You also have data on the step where each person quit.

options.text: Redesign the whole form with a fresh, modern look
options.feedback: You use up two weeks and the form looks better. Completion barely moves, because the questions that made people quit are still there.

options.text: Find the exact step where people quit, and fix that first
options.feedback: You learn where the leak is before you spend anything. A small fix at the right step usually beats big changes everywhere.

options.text: Add a 15% discount on the first clean
options.feedback: A few more people push through. But every booking now earns less, and the step that drives people away hasn't changed.

cards.eyebrow: Say you chose to find the leak
cards.title: Half the people who reach one step quit there.
body: The home-details step loses the most people. The package step comes next. Those are the two places to fix first.

cards.title: Fourteen questions before a price.
body: The home-details step asks about rooms, bathrooms, floor types, pets, parking, alarm codes and more. Your cleaners do use these answers.
But only three of them change the price. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the three price questions now and collect the rest after booking
options.feedback: Far fewer people quit at this step. Your team still gets the details by text or email once the customer has booked.

options.text: Keep all 14 questions, but add a progress bar
options.feedback: People can see the end, so a few more finish. But you still ask for the same amount of work, and most still quit.

options.text: Keep all 14 questions, but make every one optional
options.feedback: More people pass, but many skip the price questions too. Quotes come out wrong, and cleaners arrive with too little time booked.

cards.title: Nine packages, one tired customer.
body: Say you chose three questions. Now the package step leaks most. Customers choose from nine packages, including basic, standard, deep, move-out and eco versions.
Most people who do book pick Standard, every two weeks.

image.label: Nine cluttered package cards shrinking to three clear ones
image.brief: 왼쪽에는 겹쳐진 9장의 패키지 카드(Basic, Standard, Deep, Move-out, Eco 등)가 어지럽게 놓여 있고, 오른쪽에는 깔끔한 카드 3장만 나란히 있음. 가운데 카드에 'Most chosen' 라벨. 로고는 쓰지 않음.

options.text: Keep all nine and add a detailed comparison table
options.feedback: Careful shoppers like it. Most people now face even more to read, and many still leave to think about it.

options.text: Show three packages, mark Standard as most chosen, put the rest under 'More options'
options.feedback: Choosing gets easy, and more people get past this step. Customers who need a move-out or eco clean can still find one.
The step gets fast, but people with real needs, such as a move-out clean, can't find what they came for. They call a competitor.

cards.title: Office managers who never book a visit.
body: Say you chose three packages, and home bookings climb. Then your office-cleaning team asks for help.
Businesses request a quote online, but you must see the site before quoting. The form ends with "We'll be in touch to arrange a visit." Many requests go cold after missed calls and slow emails.

image.label: An office manager's screen with a suggested visit time already filled in
image.brief: 사무실 책상 위 노트북 화면. 견적 양식 끝에 'Suggested visit: Tue 10:00 · Change' 버튼이 미리 채워져 있음. 옆에는 울리지만 받지 않는 전화기. 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

options.text: Suggest a visit time, pre-filled and easy to change
options.feedback: Most people simply accept the suggested time, so the visit gets booked in one step. Anyone who needs a different time changes it in two clicks.

options.text: Show a blank calendar and let them pick any slot
options.feedback: Better than waiting for a call. But a blank calendar is one more decision, and some office managers put it off and never come back.

options.text: Pre-tick a box that signs them up for a 12-month contract after the visit
options.feedback: A few contracts come from people who didn't notice the box. Then come cancellations, angry emails and a reputation for tricks.

cards.title: An easier flow is not always a better one.
body: Fewer questions mean less information up front. If the alarm code or pet details never arrive, the first clean goes badly. Ask for the missing details soon after booking.
A default helps only when it's the choice most customers would make anyway. If a default serves you at the customer's expense, you win one sale and lose their trust.
cards.softwareNote: Software sign-ups leak the same way, through long forms, too many plans and blank setup screens. Measure drop-off at each step, ask only what the first session needs, and pre-fill sensible settings that users can change.

cards.title: Find the leaking step, then fix that step.
body: Each decision used one idea from this unit:
list: **Decision 1 · Find the step:** measure where people quit before you change anything
**Decision 2 · Friction:** ask only what you need now and collect the rest later
**Decision 3 · Choice overload:** show a few clear options and keep the rest one click away
**Decision 4 · Defaults:** pre-fill the choice most people would make, and make it easy to change
cards.callout: **Try it today:** go through your own booking or sign-up process as a customer would. Count the questions and choices someone faces before they see a price.
